crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Credit Scoring with Alternative Data
children.blurb: Credit scoring with alternative data covers models that estimate a borrower's likelihood of default or creditworthiness using information beyond the traditional credit bureau file.

children.name: Covenant Extraction
children.blurb: Covenant extraction is the work of turning the terms of credit agreements, indentures, and loan documents into structured data that a credit team can query and monitor.

children.name: Predicting Distress and Default
children.blurb: Predicting distress and default covers the estimation of a borrower's or issuer's likelihood of failing to meet debt obligations over horizons set by the portfolio or regulatory context.

children.name: Modelling the Yield Curve
children.blurb: Modelling the yield curve covers the estimation of the term structure of interest rates from market prices, including spot rates, forward rates, discount factors and par yields.

children.name: Stress Testing Structured Credit
children.blurb: Stress testing structured credit covers securitized products such as RMBS, CMBS, ABS, CLOs and CDOs, and the tranches that sit on top of underlying pools.

sections.body: Fixed income and credit risk is the work of estimating whether borrowers will pay, how much lenders can recover, and how prices of bonds and loans respond to changing rates and defaults. AI is used in credit scoring with alternative data, where models read transaction records, utility payments, and other non traditional signals to score borrowers who lack long credit histories. It is used in covenant extraction, where language models read loan agreements and indentures to pull out financial maintenance tests, baskets, and triggers. It is used in predicting distress and default, where classifiers and survival models estimate the probability that a company or issuer will miss payments or enter bankruptcy. It is also used in modelling the yield curve, where statistical and machine learning methods fit the term structure of interest rates and forecast its movements. In stress testing structured credit, AI helps simulate how pools of mortgages, auto loans, or corporate loans behave under severe economic scenarios.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Credit scoring with alternative data has moved into production at many lenders, though regulators still ask for explainability and fair lending checks. Covenant extraction is partly solved for common clauses, but long documents, unusual definitions, and cross references still cause errors, so human review remains common. Predicting distress and default is harder than scoring consumer credit because public defaults are rare, data is noisy, and labels arrive late. Yield curve modelling has strong statistical baselines, and machine learning often adds modest gains rather than a complete replacement. Stress testing structured credit is computationally heavy and depends on assumptions about correlation and recovery, so results are scenarios, not forecasts, and the site's 222 compliance and regulation pages reflect how much of this work is shaped by rules and reporting duties.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section divide the work into five connected tasks. Credit Scoring with Alternative Data is the entry point for consumer and small business lending, where non traditional data expands who can be scored. Covenant Extraction is the document layer, turning legal language into structured terms that feed monitoring and early warning. Predicting Distress and Default is the issuer level layer, estimating the chance of missed payments and bankruptcy for companies and sovereigns. Modelling the Yield Curve is the rates layer, giving discount factors and scenarios that price fixed income instruments and shape credit spreads. Stress Testing Structured Credit is the portfolio layer, taking the outputs of the other pages and asking how securitised pools hold up under shocks. A reader would go to the first for scoring methods, the second for contract parsing, the third for default models, the fourth for term structure methods, and the fifth for scenario design and structured finance risk.
